precepts.label: Deuteronomy 27:15-26
precepts.why:
“For as many as are of the works of the law are under the curse.” The works of the law, in Galatians 3:2, 3:5, 3:10 and 2:16, is sacrifice, as in Nehemiah 10:33. Under the curse means under the curse of the covenant. And “Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them” is Paul quoting Deuteronomy 27.

What does that curse mean? “Cursed be the man that maketh any graven or molten image”, “And all the people shall answer and say, Amen.” Can he atone for it, reconcile with God, find justification? What animal can he use? None. Under the old covenant you get death. That is what cursed means.

So it goes all the way down. “Cursed be he that setteth light by his father or his mother”: disrespects, curses or strikes them. “Cursed be he that removeth his neighbour’s landmark.” The so-called white man has removed the neighbor's landmark: America is a stolen landmark, Africa is a stolen landmark, Australia is a stolen landmark. How can he atone when the land is still in his possession? He can't; he sits on stolen land. “Cursed be he that lieth with his father’s wife”, his stepmother. “Cursed be he that lieth with any manner of beast.” “Cursed be he that lieth with his sister”, “with his mother in law.” “Cursed be he that smiteth his neighbour secretly”: kills his brother secretly and does not get caught. “Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person”: a hitman, a mercenary.

After each one, “all the people shall say, Amen”: we all agreed to it. Then “Cursed be he that confirmeth not all the words of this law to do them”, which is exactly what Paul quotes. None of these could be atoned for with an animal. It is death all throughout.

That is why those of the works of the law are under the curse. We confirmed to do everything under that covenant of sacrifices, and if you violate a law that no animal can cover, you get the curse, which is death.

precepts.label: Acts 13:38-39
precepts.why:
“But that no man is justified by the law in the sight of God, it is evident: for, The just shall live by faith.” Justified by the law here is the same law as the works of the law in verses 2, 5 and 10 and in Galatians 2:16: the law of sacrifice.

Paul preached the same thing in Acts 13: “Be it known unto you therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins: And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.” Through Christ is preached the forgiveness of sins, and all that believe in Christ's death are justified from all things, all sins.

Could you receive justification from all things under Moses? No, because animals do not atone for all things. Does Christ's death atone for all things, reconcile us from all things, justify us from all things? Yes. That is the difference.

And the law is not of faith because faith came first. “The man that doeth them shall live in them”: the man who does the sacrifices lives until he commits a sin worthy of death, and then he cannot live anymore. The just live by faith in the one whose death covers what no animal could.

precepts.label: John 11:49-52
precepts.why:
“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law.” Some people read right past that. What is the curse of the law? Death. But you need a scripture to back up what you say, and John 11 is it.

“And one of them, named Caiaphas, being the high priest that same year, said unto them, Ye know nothing at all, Nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not.” The whole nation, all twelve tribes, perishing: that is the curse of the law. All twelve tribes broke the first covenant, and by that default we were all worthy of death. When Christ died, he took that curse upon himself for us. That is “being made a curse for us”: dying for us.

“And this spake he not of himself: but being high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus should die for that nation; And not for that nation only.” Not for Judah only, “but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.” Gather together in one is reconciliation, at-one-ment, atonement.

So Christ died for Judah and for Israel, all twelve tribes. Those scattered abroad are the ones Paul was going to among the heathen, among the Gentiles, while being called Gentiles themselves. That is how “the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ.”

precepts.label: Deuteronomy 21:22-23
precepts.why:
“for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree”. That is written in Deuteronomy 21: “And if a man have committed a sin worthy of death, and he be to be put to death, and thou hang him on a tree: His body shall not remain all night upon the tree, but thou shalt in any wise bury him that day; (for he that is hanged is accursed of God;) that thy land be not defiled.” Hanging was capital punishment among us.

So Christ took on the curses for us, the punishment and consequence of violating that covenant, when he was hung. Some say he wasn't hung, he was nailed to a cross. But if you are nailed to a wooden pole, you are hanging by your hands and feet. That is a lynching. He was hung for hours.

Peter calls it the same thing, twice: “The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree.” And again, “whom they slew and hanged on a tree.” They hung Christ on a tree, on wood, a cross. Christ died a black man's death.

Do you think the lynchings among our people were a coincidence, when the white man hung us from trees and lamps and bridges? People have been hung from time to time, but not to the capacity we have been hung; it was enforced all around among us. The curse of the tree came on our people, and Christ bore that same curse to redeem us from it, “That the blessing of Abraham might come on the Gentiles through Jesus Christ; that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.”

precepts.label: Romans 8:3
precepts.why:
“But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed.” The we is Israel, kept under the law of sacrifice until Christ came on the scene and died for us, the same as Hebrews 9 saying it was imposed until the time of reformation. “Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ”: our mentor, our stepping stone, the placeholder for Christ's body being offered in the end. “that we might be justified by faith”: Christ's death justifies us, not the law of sacrifice.

What was it that could not justify? “For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh”. The law referred to here is animal sacrifice. Weak through the flesh means through our flesh, and it involves the animals as well. “God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh”.

He did away with our condemnation by his own death. As Caiaphas said, it is expedient that one man should die for the people, that the whole nation perish not. Christ ended the condemnation of all twelve tribes by dying on the cross.

So “after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster.” Christ has come and gone, and we are all the children of God by faith in Christ, not by animal sacrifice. That was the bewitching earlier in the chapter: that you could be justified without Christ, and all you needed was an animal.

precepts.label: Hebrews 7:18-19
precepts.why:
“For there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof.” What commandment was annulled? Sacrifice. It was annulled for its weakness and unprofitableness, done away in Christ. That is the same weakness as Romans 8:3, the law that was weak through the flesh.

“For the law made nothing perfect”. What law made nothing perfect? Hebrews 10:1 said the sacrifices offered could not make the comers thereunto perfect. It made no man perfect. “but the bringing in of a better hope did; by the which we draw nigh unto God.” Not what, but who: Christ is the better hope, and through him we draw nigh unto God.

That is why “after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster”. The schoolmaster, the law of sacrifice, was disannulled, and the ye who were kept under it, whether called Jews or Greeks, bond or free, male or female, are the same people of God in Christ.

“And if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.” The promise pertains to the Israelites. All nations are not the children of promise. If they are, name the nation God calls his people in the old covenant. Isaiah 19 says Egypt my people and Assyria the work of my hands, but Isaiah 27, Isaiah 11 and Zechariah 10 show that means the children of Israel gathered out of Egypt and Assyria. That is called precepts.

precepts.label: Hebrews 9:9-10
precepts.why:
“But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed.” Who was kept under the law? “Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law”. We were locked into that covenant until Christ came, died, and granted us liberty.

What was it we were kept under? Hebrews gives an example of the works of the law: “Which was a figure for the time then present, in which were offered both gifts and sacrifices, that could not make him that did the service perfect, as pertaining to the conscience”. The sacrifices could not make him that did them perfect, because sin was already in us since Adam. So the animals had to be temporary.

“Which stood only in meats and drinks”: meat offerings and drink offerings. These are the works of the law read all through Galatians, in 2:16, 3:2, 3:5 and 3:10-11. “and divers washings”: baptisms. “and carnal ordinances”: the traditions of the Pharisees. “imposed on them until the time of reformation.” Forced upon them until the time of reformation, which is the faith that should afterwards be revealed, when Christ came and did away with all of it.

So “the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ”. The schoolmaster was sacrifice. The sacrificing of animals was a foreshadowing of Christ's death, preparing us for his body. It was temporary, because we grew weary and rebellious behind it and would all have been condemned through it. “But after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster”: no longer under the law of sacrifice.

precepts.label: 2 Maccabees 6:1,6
precepts.why:
“There is neither Jew nor Greek”. Christians read it like a soft effeminate man, neither Jew nor Greek, brother, and say it means anybody. The people of Christianity have no idea about history. Why does Paul reference Greeks?

“Not long after this the king sent an old man of Athens to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers, and not to live after the laws of God”. Your law, your culture and your race go hand in hand with God. The Bible says love your neighbour as yourself; that is law. Deny your race and you deny your laws; deny your law and you deny your God.

“Neither was it lawful for a man to keep sabbath days or ancient fasts, or to profess himself at all to be a Jew.” It was basically illegal under the order of the king to call yourself a Jew or keep Jewish customs. So over time we became Greeks, Gentiles.

That is who Paul is writing to. The ye that were kept under the law in verse 23 are the same ye called Jews and Greeks, bond and free, male and female. Do not escape that context. Whatever your title or status in that present world, Jew or Greek, free like Paul or bond like others, “ye are all one in Christ Jesus”: all God's chosen people.

precepts.label: 2 Maccabees 4:7-9
precepts.why:
How did Israelites become Greeks? “But after the death of Seleucus, when Antiochus, called Epiphanes, took the kingdom, Jason the brother of Onias laboured underhand to be high priest”. Jason was a wicked Israelite who changed his name to Jason, a Greek name. He sought underhandedly to be high priest against his brother Onias, a righteous man, using money to gain authority and leadership. When a man seeks leadership, he usually is not meant to be a leader at all.

“Promising unto the king by intercession three hundred and threescore talents of silver, and of another revenue eighty talents”. He bribed the king of the Greeks, the white man, to force his brother out of position and put him in. “Beside this, he promised to assign an hundred and fifty more, if he might have licence to set him up a place for exercise”, a gym, “and for the training up of youth in the fashions of the heathen”: training the Israelite youth in the culture of the Greeks.

“and to write them of Jerusalem by the name of Antiochians.” He registered the Israelites of Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch, the Antioch in Turkey that Paul writes about. Becoming Antiochians was a betrayal of the ancestral laws and a shift to the Greek way of life, and that cultural tension triggered the Maccabean revolt. Antiochian and Greek are the same.

So when Paul says “There is neither Jew nor Greek”, he is writing to the descendants of those same people. Whether called Jew or Greek, “if ye be Christ’s, then are ye Abraham’s seed, and heirs according to the promise.” The heirs are Israelites, to whom pertain the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law and the promises.

precepts.label: Hebrews 9:15
precepts.why:
“But when the fulness of the time was come”, the time appointed of the Father, “God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons.” Who did Christ come to redeem? Them that were under the law. The we is the same we of chapter 3 that were kept under the law, and the adoption pertains to Israel.

Hebrews is the nail in the coffin: “And for this cause he is the mediator of the new testament, that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance.” Christ is the mediator of the new testament by means of his death, hanging on the cross. Redemption is the redeeming, and he died for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first testament.

Who was under the first testament? Israel. So those Christ redeemed are those who were under the law, the called who receive the promise of eternal inheritance: the heirs.

“And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father. Wherefore thou art no more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ.” When Christ died we were no longer servants but sons of the Father, and heirs through his Son.

precepts.label: Romans 8:3
precepts.why:
“But now, after that ye have known God, or rather are known of God, how turn ye again to the weak and beggarly elements, whereunto ye desire again to be in bondage?” We know the true God now, not a pagan one, and we are known of God because Christ died for us. Verse 3 said we were in bondage under the elements of the world; verse 9 calls them weak and beggarly elements. It is the same bondage the false brethren of chapter 2 wanted to bring us back into. So what are they?

Some say we keep saying law of sacrifice and it does not say that. But it does call it weak. “For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh”. Weak through the flesh means weak through our sin, through us.

What could the law not do? Hebrews 9:9 says the gifts and sacrifices “could not make him that did the service perfect, as pertaining to the conscience”. The sacrificing of animals could not make us perfect. That is what the law could not do, and that is the weak in the weak and beggarly elements.

So God sent his own Son to do what the animals could not, and to turn back to animal sacrifice after knowing God is to desire again to be in bondage.

precepts.label: Hebrews 7:18-19
precepts.why:
Paul calls them “weak and beggarly elements”. Hebrews calls the same thing weak: “For there is verily a disannulling of the commandment going before for the weakness and unprofitableness thereof.” The disannulling is of animal sacrifice. What made it weak and unprofitable? “For the law made nothing perfect”, including the man's conscience, “but the bringing in of a better hope did; by the which we draw nigh unto God.” That better hope is Christ.

Hebrews 10 says it again: “For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect.” It could not make those who offered them perfect.

So the weak and beggarly elements are the sacrificing of animals. They were unprofitable because we were too sinful to keep maintaining them.

That is why verse 10 says “Ye observe days, and months, and times, and years”. Ezekiel 45:17 shows that it was the prince's part to give burnt offerings, meat offerings and drink offerings in the feasts, the new moons, the sabbaths and all solemnities, to make reconciliation for the house of Israel. Colossians 2:16 matches it: meat, drink, holyday, new moon and sabbath days: “Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.” On each of those days you had to sacrifice, and Christ is the body, the sacrifice for all of those things. The Galatians were turning back to observing those days by the weak and beggarly elements.

precepts.label: Acts 15:1-5
precepts.why:
Who was bewitching the Galatians back into bondage? “And certain men which came down from Judea taught the brethren, and said, Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved.” After the manner of Moses, sacrifice followed circumcision, on the eighth day. To be circumcised after the manner of Moses meant going back to sacrifice.

“When therefore Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and disputation with them, they determined that Paul and Barnabas, and certain other of them, should go up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.” These men came from Judea infiltrating and causing confusion, saying you have to sacrifice.

“But there rose up certain of the sect of the Pharisees which believed, saying, That it was needful to circumcise them, and to command them to keep the law of Moses.” The Pharisees came in as believers, part of the church, and were imposing that you had to sacrifice according to the manner of Moses. These are the same false brethren brought in unawares that Galatians addresses, who came in privily to spy out our liberty and bring us into bondage.

As the movement grew, the Pharisees went into the churches to win them back to temple law. Paul said he profited in the Jews' religion; people bringing animals was their bread and butter. They were saying to hell with what Christ did, you need an animal for atonement. Paul's answer: if you do, you are condemned, because the temple would be destroyed.

precepts.label: Hebrews 9:22
precepts.why:
“And almost all things are by the law purged with blood”. Almost, not all. So be mindful of always saying blood sacrifice, because the heathen are going to come with that. Not every sin offering was blood, because some among us were poor and could not bring a blood sacrifice.

Leviticus shows it: “But if he be not able to bring two turtledoves, or two young pigeons, then he that sinned shall bring for his offering the tenth part of an ephah of fine flour for a sin offering; he shall put no oil upon it, neither shall he put any frankincense thereon: for it is a sin offering.” The priest took his handful of it as a memorial and burned it on the altar.

And the main example was obedience: “He that keepeth the law bringeth offerings enough: he that taketh heed to the commandment offereth a peace offering. He that requiteth a good turn offereth fine flour; and he that giveth alms sacrificeth praise. To depart from wickedness is a thing pleasing to the Lord; and to forsake unrighteousness is a propitiation.” A propitiation is reconciliation. When you depart from sin and keep God's commandments, that is sacrifice enough.

Israel never got there. Israel thought, I can sin all I want and sacrifice all I want, and I'm good. We were children under the schoolmaster, sacrificing and sinning again, going into slavery and out and back again. The Lord said enough of that, and sent his Son. That is why turning back to the weak and beggarly elements is turning back to bondage.

precepts.label: Psalms 148:14
precepts.why:
“Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, to the saints which are at Ephesus”. To the who? To the saints. So we must go into the Bible and figure out who the saints are.

“He also exalteth the horn of his people”: his people, the Israelites. “the praise of all his saints”: his saints. “even of the children of Israel, a people near unto him.” If you did not know, even means indeed. Indeed, of the children of Israel.

So the saints of God are the children of Israel, the people near unto him. When Paul writes to the saints which are at Ephesus, he is writing to Israelites living in Ephesus, not to everybody in the city. That is where the understanding of Ephesians has to start.

precepts.label: Psalms 50:5
precepts.why:
Paul writes “to the saints which are at Ephesus”, so who are the saints? The Lord says: “Gather my saints together unto me; those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice.”

So the only saints in the Bible are the ones that made a covenant with God by sacrifice. That is Israel, the people who made the covenant with him. It did not change. It did not go away. That is who the saints are.

So when Paul opens his letter to the saints, he is speaking to the covenant people, the ones God gathers unto himself. The letter to the Ephesians is written to Israel, and it has to be read that way.

precepts.label: Deuteronomy 33:1-3
precepts.why:
“And this is the blessing, wherewith Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death.” Who? The children of Israel. “And he said, The Lord came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir unto them; he shined forth from mount Paran, and he came with ten thousands of saints”. Of who? Of saints. When we were liberated out of Egypt, he called them the saints.

“from his right hand went a fiery law for them.” That is how you know it is not talking about the mixed multitude among them: the fiery law went to the children of Israel only. “Yea, he loved the people; all his saints are in thy hand”: all these saints, the children of Israel, are in his hand. “and they sat down at thy feet; every one shall receive of thy words.”

So the saints are the children of Israel, the ones who received the law from his right hand. When Paul writes “to the saints which are at Ephesus”, he means the same people Moses blessed: Israel.

precepts.label: Isaiah 11:11-13
precepts.why:
Isaiah shows what the “middle wall of partition” of Ephesians 2:14 looks like: the hatred, the enmity, the envy and the vexation between the two kingdoms.

“And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.” Has this happened yet? No. We are waiting on this second coming, waiting to be delivered again. That is why unification is so important: we have to go back to all these places, because our people are there. The Bible says they are in Assyria, in Egypt, in Pathros, in Cush, in Elam, and in the islands of the sea. We have a lot of work to do.

“And he shall set up an ensign for the nations, and shall assemble the outcasts of Israel, and gather together the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.” The outcasts are those who were kept afar off, living amongst the other nations as heathens, like Hellenized Jews. These are the ones Paul calls those “who sometimes were far off” and are now “made nigh by the blood of Christ.”

“The envy also of Ephraim shall depart, and the adversaries of Judah shall be cut off: Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not vex Ephraim.” The envy of Ephraim, the northern kingdom, is the wall of partition, and it is going to be gone. No more division: light skinned against dark skinned, look at your hair, look at my hair; the northern kingdom looking at us and us looking at them. Yes, Esau touched the northern kingdom; the southern kingdom has been through changes too. We look different today, but we are all the same people.

That wall is what Christ tore down. “He is our peace, who hath made both one”: the two sticks, Judah and Ephraim, made one, and right now in the congregation northern and southern kingdom are back together again.

thread.label: Ephesians 2:12
thread.text: That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:

classes.title: Christians Don't Understand Ephesians 2

precepts.label: 2 Chronicles 15:9
precepts.why:
Paul says “at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise”. Who were the strangers? Chronicles shows it: Asa “gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and the strangers with them out of Ephraim and Manasseh, and out of Simeon: for they fell to him out of Israel in abundance, when they saw that the Lord his God was with him.”

The strangers out of Ephraim and Manasseh. That is the northern kingdom, and they were called strangers. Israelites, called strangers.

The literal definition of Gentiles is nation. How can you in time past be another nation? How can you in time past be another race? Go to sleep Japanese, wake up Arab? That does not make any sense. It only makes sense in Christianity. But when you read that Israelites of the northern kingdom were called strangers, Ephesians 2:12 makes sense: the strangers were Israel.

precepts.label: Hosea 4:17
precepts.why:
Why were Ephraim and the northern kingdom called strangers? Hosea says it: “Ephraim is joined to idols: let him alone.”

So at one point the northern kingdom was not a part of the commonwealth of Israel. Why? Ephraim joined himself to idols and was let alone. They became strangers; they became alienated from the commonwealth of Israel. That is what Paul means by “aliens from the commonwealth of Israel”: not another race of people, but Israelites who were cut off for their idolatry.

It is very basic and simple. All you have to do is read. Blessed is he that readeth.

precepts.label: Ezekiel 37:11
precepts.why:
Paul says they were “having no hope, and without God in the world.” Who was without hope? Ezekiel shows it: “Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel: behold, they say, Our bones are dried, and our hope is lost: we are cut off for our parts.”

They said it themselves: no hope. So Israel was the one without hope. “we are cut off for our parts”: we were alienated from the commonwealth. The dry bones are the whole house of Israel, not another nation.

So every part of Ephesians 2:12 lines up with Israel. The ones cut off, the ones with their hope lost, the aliens from the commonwealth, were the house of Israel itself, and that is who the letter is speaking to.

precepts.label: Romans 9:4
precepts.why:
Paul says the same people were “strangers from the covenants of promise”. But to whom do the covenants belong? Romans says it: they “are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises”.

“to whom pertaineth the adoption”: that means the coming back; they were brought back. “and the covenants”: the covenants, the old and the new, only belong to the Israelites. The promises belong to them too.

So you can only be a stranger from a covenant that was yours to begin with. You were strangers from the covenants of promise for a time, but it was always for you. Ephesians 2:12 is Israel cut off and then brought back through Christ, not the nations being added in.

precepts.label: Ephesians 1:1
precepts.why:
Pastor Philip Anthony Mitchell preached that black people use their ethnicity as an idol, that black people don't like white people for something they cannot control, and that Ephesians 2 is about joining blacks and whites together through Christ into one family. Did he forget about slavery? He leans on Ephesians 2:14: “For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us.” So we have to deal with the us. Who is Paul talking about?

Paul uses two specific words, our and us. To know who they are, go back to the top of the letter and see who it was written to: “Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, to the saints which are at Ephesus, and to the faithful in Christ Jesus.”

The letter was written to the saints which are at Ephesus. So the question becomes, who are the saints according to the holy scriptures? Answer that, and you know who the our and the us are in chapter 2. It is not blacks and whites coming together.

precepts.label: Psalms 148:14
precepts.why:
“He also exalteth the horn of his people, the praise of all his saints; even of the children of Israel, a people near unto him. Praise ye the Lord.” The saints are the children of Israel.

When the brothers were dealing with Fred Price and brought out the scripture about the saints, he asked, are you saying all the saints in the New Testament have to be the children of Israel? Yes. He said he didn't necessarily see that. But you know what Christianity has never been able to do? Show another definition of saints in the scripture. They are not going to be able to. The only saints in the scriptures are the twelve tribes of Israel.

So the saints which are at Ephesus are Israelites, and the us of Ephesians 2 is the nation of Israel. This isn't talking about blacks and whites coming together, like Pastor Mitchell was saying.

precepts.label: Acts 13:17
precepts.why:
Ephesians 2:12 says that at that time they were “without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.” Christians will say, well, you have to deal with those strangers. So let's see who the strangers are.

“The God of this people of Israel chose our fathers, and exalted the people when they dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt.” The book of Acts is saying that the God of Israel chose our fathers, so the people Paul was speaking to in Antioch were Israelites. And who dwelt as strangers in the land of Egypt? The nation of Israel.

So those strangers are the Israelites. The scripture calls Israel strangers, and that is who Ephesians is speaking to when it says strangers from the covenants of promise.

precepts.label: 1 Peter 1:1
precepts.why:
“Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the strangers scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.” Peter writes to the strangers, and the strangers are Israel, scattered abroad.

Put the map up and focus on Asia, which is Asia Minor. There you see Ephesus, and right next to it Colosse. That is what we are dealing with: the letter to the Colossians, and since Pastor Mitchell brought up Ephesus, which is right there in Asia next to Colosse, the letter to the Ephesians too.

So the saints at Ephesus and the strangers Peter wrote to are the same people: Israelites scattered through Asia. When Paul says they were “strangers from the covenants of promise”, he is writing to scattered Israel, not to the nations.

precepts.label: Romans 9:4-5
precepts.why:
Christians never address the covenants of promise. The only time the Lord made a covenant with all nations was in Genesis 9, when he said he would not destroy the world by water any more. In regards to the covenants, the Lord made covenant with Abraham, and through his seed, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He never made any other covenants with other nations.

Paul says it plainly: “Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises; Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came.” The Bible is letting you know that Christ came for the Israelites, and he made the covenants of promise for the Israelites. No other nation.

The question was even put to ChatGPT live in class: did God ever enter into a covenant with all nations or only Israel, answered with KJV scriptures. Its answer: God made a universal covenant with all humanity through Noah after the flood; the covenant of the law at Sinai was only with Israel, not with all nations; and the new covenant as prophesied is with the house of Israel and the house of Judah. They know that, but they try to force this all nations could be saved doctrine. It is not in the Bible.

So “strangers from the covenants of promise” can only be read one way: the covenant of promise is only with Israel.

precepts.label: Jeremiah 46:27
precepts.why:
Ephesians 2:13: “But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.” Who was afar off? We deal with precepts. These Christians like to say, let's go to the Greek, let's go to this book, let's go to that. We stick to the scriptures and stay within our book.

“But fear not thou, O my servant Jacob, and be not dismayed, O Israel: for, behold, I will save thee from afar off.” It is Israel who is afar off.

It's really that simple. The ones who were far off and are made nigh by the blood of Christ are Israel. Then verse 14: “For he is our peace.” Our peace, not everybody's peace. Reading from verse 12 down to verse 14, the our becomes plain: these Ephesians in Ephesus are Israelites scattered in Ephesus.

precepts.label: Isaiah 9:6-8
precepts.why:
Ephesians says “he is our peace”, so go to the prophecy of the Prince of Peace. “For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given”: unto us, possessive again. “and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace.”

“Of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end, upon the throne of David, and upon his kingdom, to order it, and to establish it with judgment and with justice from henceforth even for ever.” When it's time for Christ to return and the Israelites to reign, there is not going to be any end to it. “The zeal of the Lord of hosts will perform this.”

Then: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it hath lighted upon Israel.” So our peace is Israel's peace. Christ is the peace that brings both nations, the southern and the northern kingdom, back together. That is the both he made one.

precepts.label: Ezekiel 37:21-22
precepts.why:
“For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us.” Remember the animal sacrifice that was against us. When Christ came on the scene, he abolished animal sacrifice. And it was never prophesied that Israel would be joined back together through animal sacrifice, but only through Jesus the Christ.

“Thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I will take the children of Israel from among the heathen, whither they be gone, and will gather them on every side, and bring them into their own land.” He gathers the children of Israel from among the heathen, so you would have Israelites living in places like Galatia, Ephesus and Colosse.

“And I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all: and they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all.” That is what Ephesians 2:14 means by made both one.

So he is our peace: the Israelites' peace. These Christians in America do not know what they are talking about. Turning Ephesians 2 into blacks and whites coming together is a racist lie. Christianity is nothing but white supremacy, because it is not backed up with the Bible whatsoever.

thread.label: Ephesians 2:13
thread.text: But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.

classes.title: Christians Don't Understand Ephesians 2

precepts.label: Daniel 9:7
precepts.why:
Ephesians 2:13 says “ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.” Who was far off? Who was once close, and then got distant, pushed away, cut off? Daniel answers it in his prayer.

“O Lord, righteousness belongeth unto thee, but unto us confusion of faces, as at this day; to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and unto all Israel, that are near, and that are far off, through all the countries whither thou hast driven them, because of their trespass that they have trespassed against thee.” That are where? That are far off. The far off are Israel, driven into all the countries because of their trespass against the Lord.

So the far off of Ephesians are not other nations. They are Israel, both near and far off. Israel said, we are cut off for our parts, we have no hope. But now they do have hope, through Christ: the ones who were far off are made nigh by his blood.

thread.label: Ephesians 2:14
thread.text: For he is our peace, who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us;

classes.title: Christians Don't Understand Ephesians 2

precepts.label: Ezekiel 37:22
precepts.why:
“For he is our peace, who hath made both one.” He is the peace of the saints Paul writes to in Ephesians 1:1. You have to know history to understand this verse, because why does it say both? Is it only talking about Jews and Gentiles? What happened in the history?

Ezekiel shows it: “And I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all: and they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all.” One king: Christ. No more two nations.

That is the both that he made one: the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom. Jew and Gentile, circumcision and uncircumcision, are those same two kingdoms. When those two kingdoms were against each other they were at odds, and that hatred was the middle wall of partition. But the Lord said there is going to be peace, and Christ is that peace, making the two into one again.

precepts.label: Ezekiel 37:26
precepts.why:
“Moreover I will make a covenant of peace with them; it shall be an everlasting covenant with them: and I will place them, and multiply them, and will set my sanctuary in the midst of them for evermore.”

This is the same chapter where the Lord promises to make the two kingdoms one nation with one king. With that promise comes a covenant of peace. And Ephesians 2:14 says, “For he is our peace, who hath made both one.” The covenant of peace Ezekiel spoke of is Christ.

So in one chapter of Ezekiel we get all of the information and all of the understanding of Ephesians 2: the two kingdoms made one, one king over them all, and an everlasting covenant of peace. Paul is not speaking about the other nations joining Israel; he is speaking about the fulfilling of this prophecy for the house of Israel.

thread.label: Ephesians 2:15
thread.text: Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;

classes.title: Christians Don't Understand Ephesians 2

precepts.label: Hebrews 9:9-10
precepts.why:
Ephesians 2:14 speaks of “the middle wall of partition between us.” What is that wall? The next verse explains it: “Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances.” A Christian’s head just blew off. They do not know what that is talking about. What are those commandments contained in ordinances?

Hebrews tells us. The tabernacle service “was a figure for the time then present, in which were offered both gifts and sacrifices, that could not make him that did the service perfect, as pertaining to the conscience; Which stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation.”

Carnal ordinances. These are the commandments contained in ordinances: the law of sacrifice. That was the enmity, and that was the wall of partition between the two kingdoms. It was imposed only until the time of reformation, and Christ abolished it in his flesh, so that there is no more fighting over where and how to sacrifice.

thread.label: Ephesians 2:15-16
thread.text: Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;

classes.title: Christians Don't Understand Ephesians 2

precepts.label: 2 Esdras 6:54-56
precepts.why:
Ephesians says he made “of twain one new man, so making peace,” the same twain made one in Ezekiel 37, and the peace is the covenant of peace of Ezekiel 37:26. Then: “that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross.” Words are important, Christians; the Bible is full of them. Reconcile is a verb that means to restore friendly relations. So when was God ever on friendly terms with the other nations?

Ezra answers: “And after these, Adam also, whom thou madest lord of all thy creatures: of him come we all, and the people also whom thou hast chosen. All this have I spoken before thee, O Lord, because thou madest the world for our sakes.” He made the world for the Israelites’ sake.

“As for the other people, which also come of Adam, thou hast said that they are nothing, but be like unto spittle: and hast likened the abundance of them unto a drop that falleth from a vessel.” They are nothing. Does that sound like friendly relations? No, they never were. Isaiah 40:17 says the same thing, for anyone who does not think the Apocrypha is canon. So the reconciling of Ephesians 2 cannot be about the other nations.

precepts.label: Isaiah 63:16
precepts.why:
“Doubtless thou art our father, though Abraham be ignorant of us, and Israel acknowledge us not: thou, O Lord, art our father, our redeemer; thy name is from everlasting.” The Lord is Israel’s father and Israel’s redeemer, from everlasting.

Reconciled: reconciled who, to what? Married people get reconciled. They were together under a covenant, something happened and they broke apart, and in order to bring the marriage back together they must reconcile. That is what the word means.

The nation of Israel was once together under God, as the children of their father. Something happened: sin and the split of the kingdoms. Then Christ brought them back together. That is why Ephesians says he might “reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross”: both kingdoms brought back to the Father who was always theirs.

precepts.label: Isaiah 63:19
precepts.why:
“We are thine: thou never barest rule over them; they were not called by thy name.” Israel says to the Lord, we are yours. And of the other nations: the Lord never bore rule over them, and they were not called by His name.

So how can anyone be reconciled to a God that never owned them, never knew them, and never had them? To reconcile is to restore friendly relations that were there before. Israel was the Lord’s, called by His name, and fell away; the other nations never were His.

That is why the reconciling of Ephesians 2:16, “that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross,” belongs to Israel. The both are the two houses of Israel, the ones called by His name, brought back to the God who bore rule over them.

precepts.label: Daniel 9:24
precepts.why:
“Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city, to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most Holy.”

Thy people are the Israelites, and thy holy city is Jerusalem. Within those seventy weeks the Lord would make an end of sins and “make reconciliation for iniquity.” That reconciliation was determined upon Daniel’s people, not upon the other nations.

So when Ephesians says Christ came to “reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby,” it is the fulfilling of Daniel. Christ dying brought reconciliation to God’s people, Israel. It is very easy, very simple, very plain.
